title: Decentering the Human in the Design of Collaborative Cities
extended_summary:
This paper is a theoretical essay about how design practice should respond to socio-technical complexity in contemporary cities. The author argues that human-centered design is often too limited because it treats users as isolated individuals and tends to ignore politics, ethics, and the role of nonhuman actors in urban systems.

The paper draws on science and technology studies (STS), participatory design, speculative design, and related traditions to propose decentering the human in design. Rather than focusing on direct empirical evaluation of an intervention, it uses examples from urban technologies, prototypes, and collaborative citymaking to argue for more responsible and accountable design methods.

The context is urban technology and collaborative citymaking, with references to smart cities, infrastructure, and civic technology. The main conclusion is that designers should integrate critical, participatory, and speculative approaches to better address ethical, political, and environmental challenges and to recognize the agency of nonhuman stakeholders.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual/design-theory essay about decentering the human in collaborative citymaking, not an empirical K-12 study. It contains no direct intervention evaluation, no comparator, and no causal outcome evidence relevant to student scientific reasoning or inquiry.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper does not report measurable educational effects. It is not evidence of impact on K-12 science outcomes, so there is no basis for classifying positive educational impact.
